meta.description: Yes, Einstein said it. It comes from a 1929 Saturday Evening Post interview by G. S. Viereck — and the full line is longer than the version you know.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: Einstein said it in a 1929 interview with George Sylvester Viereck, “What Life Means to Einstein,” published in The Saturday Evening Post on 26 October 1929, and it was reprinted in Einstein’s Cosmic Religion (1931). The attribution to Einstein is genuine and well documented.

author.name: Albert Einstein
author.heading: About Albert Einstein
author.bio: Albert Einstein (1879–1955) was a German-born theoretical physicist who developed the theory of relativity and won the 1921 Nobel Prize in Physics for his work on the photoelectric effect. He gave the interview containing this line to journalist George Sylvester Viereck in 1929, at the height of his global fame. Einstein often stressed intuition and imagination as engines of scientific discovery — a theme consistent across his letters and essays.

misattribution.heading: Right author, wrong words
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Einstein is correct — this is one of the rare famous “Einstein” lines he actually said. What goes wrong is the wording and the framing.

items.why: The authentic word is “important,” per the 1929 Saturday Evening Post interview ↗. The “powerful” swap is a modern paraphrase with no primary source.

items.who: “Logic will get you from A to B. Imagination will take you everywhere.”
items.why: This second sentence is frequently fused to Einstein’s line, but it is not part of the authenticated 1929 interview text ↗ and has no known Einstein source.

misattribution.truthLine: The verified core is short and real: “Imagination is more important than knowledge,” from Einstein’s 1929 Viereck interview ↗ — everything after it that you see attached is often either paraphrase or later invention.

context.heading: What Einstein actually meant
lead: The line is real, but it is almost always quoted out of context. Einstein was not disparaging knowledge — he was talking about how discovery happens. The interviewer, George Sylvester Viereck, had just asked whether Einstein trusted his imagination more than his knowledge, and Einstein answered as a working scientist describing where new theories come from.

In his fuller reply he tied imagination to the practical business of research: knowledge is the finite set of what we already know, while imagination is the faculty that reaches past it toward what is not yet known. He called it “a real factor in scientific research,” not a rejection of rigor.
detailsBody: As printed in Cosmic Religion (1931): “I believe in intuition and inspiration. … Imagination is more important than knowledge. For knowledge is limited, whereas imagination embraces the entire world, stimulating progress, giving birth to evolution. It is, strictly speaking, a real factor in scientific research.”

The 1929 Saturday Evening Post interview phrases the follow-on sentences more tersely — “Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world” — which is why two slightly different long versions both circulate today. Both are authentically Einstein; they are simply two records of the same conversation.
